Guides

Cooking and seasoning

Herbs, a mild spice, and a spoon of oil do more for a baby’s food than salt or sugar ever will.

Findings

No salt is added before one year. That includes the cooking water, the stock, and the ‘pinch’ on a pasta sauce.
Sweetness can come from fruit. Added sugar is unnecessary before two years, and honey is unsafe before one.
Cook the family meal, then season the adult plates. Take the baby’s portion out before salt, chilli, or a salty sauce goes in.

Salt

Infant kidneys handle sodium poorly, and a salted diet teaches a preference that is hard to walk back. The practical rule is no salt in cooking for a child under one. Cheese, bread, and tinned foods already contain some; amounts of those stay modest.

Stock cubes, gravy, ham, bacon, soy sauce, and most ‘baby seasonings’ that list salt are adult shortcuts. A frozen unsalted stock cube you made yourself is a different object.

Sugar, honey, and spice

Added sugar crowds out iron-rich food and feeds decay as soon as teeth are through. Fruit, roasted pumpkin, and ripe banana are sweet enough for biscuits and porridges. Honey is not a more natural option under one year: botulism spores survive ordinary baking.

Sweet paprika, turmeric, cumin, oregano, basil, and a pinch of cinnamon are reasonable. Hot chilli and heavy black pepper are not. Cinnamon is a spice, not a spoonful; cassia cinnamon contains coumarin, so a pinch is the right dose.

One pot for everyone

Stews, sauces, and roasts can be the household meal if the baby’s share is lifted out first. Theirs is mashed or cut to the texture they can manage. Yours can then be salted.

Garlic and onion cooked in the dish are fine. Garlic or herbs stored in a bottle of oil are not: that is a known botulism setup. Add fresh herbs and the oil at the end of cooking.
